reviewGate: Maintainer scholarly review required before these construct boundaries, rivals, or predictions are treated as accepted theory.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both concern sacred public symbols, collective obligations, and moralized political identity.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: PPW scores the intensity and operational role of sacred-political order across regime types; civil religion may remain integrative without pathological escalation.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can bind individuals to an imagined political community.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: PPW requires sacred ordering of legitimacy, memory, obligation, and sacrifice; nationalism alone may be secular, instrumental, or weakly sacralized.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can organize political meaning and justify collective action.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Sacralization requires moral non-negotiability and resistance to correction, not merely a coherent political doctrine.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both help explain why institutions or claims are accepted.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Legitimation can be procedural or performance-based; sacralization marks claims as protected from ordinary bargaining or revision.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both imagine a collective actor that persists beyond individuals.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Collective immortality focuses on meaning-making around death, sacrifice, and continuity; legal personhood may be administrative without sacrificial resonance.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both link present identity to remembered predecessors and successors.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Collective memory can be plural and revisable; collective immortality claims that individual mortality is redeemed by the enduring body.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both identify an actor opposed to the order or its program.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: A sacred enemy is contaminating, existential, or profaning; an ordinary opponent remains legitimate and corrigible within political contestation.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can justify mobilization and coercive defense.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Security threat coding can rest on capability and intent; sacred-enemy coding requires moral absolutization or pollution language.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Pathological orders often authorize or normalize violence.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: PPW pathology also includes suppression of correction, frozen dysfunction, collapse, and sacrificial maladaptation; violence alone is neither necessary nor sufficient.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can involve concentrated power and restricted dissent.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Authoritarianism describes institutional control; pathology scores maladaptive sacred self-preservation against truth, correction, personhood, and flourishing.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Democratic institutions often supply opposition, accountability, and repair mechanisms.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Corrigibility measures whether an order can receive correction in practice; nominal democracy can still become uncorrigible.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Legal limits can restrain pathological self-preservation.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Rule of law is one mechanism; corrigibility also includes memory, dissent, pluralism, institutional design, and willingness to acknowledge error.

scopeConditions: The unit is an embodied political order facing a crisis interpreted through collective identity or legitimacy.
Evidence exists for institutional channels that can either suppress or receive correction.
rivalHypotheses: Material capacity alone explains escalation, collapse, or restraint.
Regime type alone explains outcome variation without sacred-political mechanisms.
External military pressure explains outcomes without internal correction capacity.
expectedObservations: Low-corrigibility cases show blocked criticism, purified loyalty demands, or escalating sacrificial justification under crisis.
Higher-corrigibility cases show public dissent, institutional review, or bounded sacrifice during comparable crisis.
counterObservations: High-corrigibility cases escalate sacrifice without suppressed correction.
Low-corrigibility cases repeatedly restrain sacrifice through ordinary institutional repair.
discriminatingPredictions: Among cases with comparable crisis intensity, correction mechanisms should better distinguish restrained reordering from sacrificial escalation than sacred-order strength alone.
Cases with strong sacred order but durable correction should show bounded sacrifice rather than automatic pathology.

scopeConditions: The case contains evidence of sacred self-preservation, correction suppression, collapse, frozen dysfunction, or successor-order transformation.
The coding distinguishes pathological process from outcome labels.
rivalHypotheses: Political pathology is reducible to observed violence or coercion.
Collapse and frozen dysfunction are ordinary institutional failure rather than sacred-order maladaptation.
Successor-order transformation is better explained by elite bargaining alone.
expectedObservations: Some high-pathology cases exhibit correction suppression or frozen maladaptation even when violence is not the dominant evidence.
Some violent cases remain analytically distinct when sacrifice is bounded or correction remains open.
counterObservations: Pathology scores track violence intensity so closely that no separate construct information remains.
Nonviolent collapse or frozen dysfunction cases lack any sacred-political mechanism.
discriminatingPredictions: A violence-only model should misclassify cases where correction suppression or collapse is central but overt killing is limited.
A PPW model should distinguish bounded wartime sacrifice from pathological sacrificial escalation by correction and sacralization evidence.
